paper_title: OmniVChat: Synthesizing, Benchmarking, and Training for Native Audio-Visual Dialogue

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We define OmniVChat (Omni Video Chat) as the task of native audio-visual dialogue between a user and an omni model. In OmniVChat, omni models directly and simultaneously receive audio and video from a user and return text. The user's query is embedded in the audio and video, without a separate text question, external captioning, or speech recognition. Direct audio-visual input reduces external latency and computation while preserving perceptual cues. However, research on OmniVChat faces two constraints: data availability and evaluation. Recordings of people using their own devices are scarce. Furthermore, a good reply often needs to account for the user's surroundings, facial expressions, and nearby objects, and such responses can be expressed in many different ways, making keyword matching unreliable for evaluating reply quality. Recent progress in agent systems and video generation makes generation for comprehension viable, which means using synthesized dialogues for training and evaluation. Therefore, we present OmniVChat-Studio, a multi-agent data engine for synthesizing single- and multi-turn audio-visual dialogues. We use synthesized dialogues to build OmniVChat-Bench, an evaluation benchmark that evaluates omni models' basic dialogue abilities across five ability categories. We also present OmniVChat-RL, a reinforcement learning reward design that jointly targets reply correctness, efficiency, and style in OmniVChat. Training Qwen3-Omni-Instruct with OmniVChat-RL on synthesized dialogues improves its performance on both OmniVChat-Bench and the human-recorded OmniVChat-Bench-Human. These gains validate the reward design and show transfer to real-world dialogues in training and evaluation.

sections.content: straints: data availability and evaluation. The ﬁrst challenge is limited data availability. Open-source recordings of people using their own devices are scarce. Noise, camera motion, and device posture create long tail of input conditions. The second challenge is evaluating reply quality. Dialogues contain complex scenes and many rare cases, where good reply should account for rich multimodal context such as the users environment, facial expressions, emotion, nearby objects and so on. Because such information can be expressed in various ways, it is difﬁcult to reliably assess reply quality through keyword matching or other rule-based methods. Few datasets and benchmarks target this native dialogue (Pourreza et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026). Models thus tend to rely on external components such as ASR cascades (Yao et al., 2026). While practical, these designs inevitably omit subtle prosody and vocal affect, and add latency, computation, and potential transcription errors. Progress in agent systems (Dorri et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2025) and video generation (Xing et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2025) makes generation for comprehension possible. This means using synthesized dialogues for training and evaluation. Our contributions are as follows. First, we present OmniVChat-Studio, controllable and extensible multi-agent data engine for synthesizing native audio-visual dialogue data at scale for training and evaluation. It contains four agents that synthesize singleand multi-turn dialogues using conﬁguration for each subcategory. Second, we introduce OmniVChat-Bench, an evaluation benchmark that evaluates omni models basic dialogue abilities across ﬁve ability categories. Each instance includes rubric. rubric contains several tiers, and each tier has one or more criteria. large language model checks whether the reply meets each criterion. Tier 0 checks whether the reply uses the users language. It gives no points, and failing it makes the rubric score zero. In later tiers, criterion earns one point only after every criterion in all earlier tiers is met. Example 1 below shows how these rules apply to one instance. Third, we present OmniVChat-RL, reinforcement learning (RL) reward design that jointly targets reply correctness, efﬁciency, and style in OmniVChat (Kaelbling et al., 1996). rubric reward for reply correctness is ﬁrst introduced using the same scoring method as in evaluation, followed by two additional reward terms for efﬁciency and style. OmniVChat-Bench-Train serves as the training corpus synthesized by OmniVChat-Studio for OmniVChat-RL, whereas OmniVChat-Bench-Human provides manually recorded benchmark for testing transfer to real-world dialogues. Fine-tuning Qwen3-OmniInstruct (Xu et al., 2025b) with OmniVChat-RL on OmniVChat-Bench-Train yields consistent performance gains across both OmniVChat-Bench and OmniVChat-Bench-Human, while simultaneously making responses more concise. These gains validate the OmniVChat-RL and demonstrate successful transfer to real-world dialogues. Given that the two benchmarks overlap across singleturn subcategories, consistent gains in these shared areas suggest that the synthetic and recorded dialogue distributions are well aligned. The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the OmniVChat-Studio framework and its single-turn and multi-turn subsystems. Section 3 presents OmniVChat-Bench for evaluating basic dialogue abilities. Section 4 presents OmniVChat-RL and the training results. Appendix provides an overview of the related work.

sections.title: 2 OMNIVCHAT-STUDIO: SYNTHESIZING DIALOGUES FROM CORPUS
sections.content: We present OmniVChat-Studio, multi-agent data engine that takes text corpus as input and synthesizes native audio-visual dialogue data. The resulting data contain rendered audio-visual clips, the corresponding reference replies, and rubrics for scoring model replies. OmniVChat-Studio consists of two subsystems, as shown in Figure 2. The single-turn subsystem on the left synthesizes one-turn dialogue data. The multi-turn subsystem on the right synthesizes sequence of dependent turns, where later turns use accepted earlier clips and dialogue as history. Both subsystems use the four agents shown in the lower-left legend of Figure 2. Each module has the same color as the agent responsible for it. The Director handles all text-based input and output tasks. The Renderer turns an accepted prompt and any media references into synchronized audiovisual clip. The Reviewer examines the rendered audio and video, writes caption and quality report, and answers focused questions when more evidence is needed. The deterministic Validator checks structured scripts or dialogue records against the conﬁgured rules and returns either pass or list of rule violations. Plan Review checks all turns and media links in separate Director call, then accepts the plan, requests revision, or discards the run. sections.content: Section 4.3 and Table 1 report transfer and model comparisons. Dialogue-State & Link Perception (DSLP) evaluates whether model understands the current state of dialogue. It covers connection status, turn boundaries, and camera orientation. For example, the model should wait when user pauses before ﬁnishing request and interpret left and right from the current camera view. Multimodal Entity Alignment (MEA) evaluates whether model connects speech with the correct visible objects and speakers. For example, the model should identify the cup indicated by gesture and address the active user when several people are speaking. Model SelfAwareness (MSA) evaluates whether model states its identity and physical limitations correctly. For example, it should not claim that it can move an object, but it can explain what the user can do instead. Anti-Hallucination (AH) evaluates whether replies remain grounded in the available audio and visual evidence. For example, the model should say when requested object is absent or correct false description of visible objects color. Emotion Recognition (ER) evaluates whether reply uses facial and vocal emotion cues. For example, worried expression and tone should lead to reply that addresses both the users emotion and request. Appendix D.4 compares model scores on matched single-turn and multi-turn subcategories. The recorded probe contains only singleturn dialogues and does not test live interruption; Appendix D.2 describes the procedures for both recording and annotating these dialogues.

sections.title: 4 OMNIVCHAT-RL: REWARDS FOR BETTER DIALOGUE
sections.content: We present OmniVChat-RL, an RL reward design that jointly targets reply correctness, efﬁciency, and style in OmniVChat. These three reply-quality signals also deﬁne the evaluation metrics. An auxiliary format term is used only during training to require valid reply. Training and evaluation use separate dialogues from the same subcategory conﬁgurations. OmniVChat-Bench measures training gains, while recorded dialogues test transfer. Matched gains can indirectly suggest aligned distributions across the shared single-turn subcategories (4.3).

sections.title: 4.1 TRAINING SETUP

OmniVChat-Bench-Train contains 5,600 training dialogues and separate 560-dialogue development split. Each dialogue and its rubric are synthesized by OmniVChat-Studio. Development scores select the checkpoint. OmniVChat-Bench-Human contains 360 human-recorded singleturn dialogues for testing transfer to real-world dialogues (recording and annotation procedures in Appendix D.2). sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We deﬁne OmniVChat as the task of native audio-visual dialogue between user and an omni model. We present OmniVChat-Studio, multi-agent data engine that synthesizes singleand multi-turn audio-visual dialogues from subcategory conﬁguration and text corpus. It supports single-turn probes and dependent turns, with reference replies and tiered rubrics. We introduce OmniVChat-Bench, an evaluation benchmark that evaluates omni models basic dialogue abilities across ﬁve ability categories. Its 17 subcategories use these rubrics. We also present OmniVChatRL, an RL reward design that jointly targets reply correctness, efﬁciency, and style in OmniVChat. Training on 5,600 synthetic dialogues raises OmniVChat-Bench from 0.465 to 0.652. The recorded OmniVChat-Bench-Human rises from 0.402 to 0.632 without training on its recordings. Mean reply length falls from 79 to 36 words. RE rises from 5.75 to 18.38, and Style rises from 0.710 to 0.992. These results support the training design and the use of synthetic data for training and evaluation in real-world dialogues. The components connect controlled synthesis, semantic evaluation, and training within one task. Agreement across synthetic and recorded dialogues indirectly suggests aligned dialogue distributions for the shared single-turn subcategories.

sections.title: B RELATED WORK
sections.content: This section reviews ﬁve research areas related to OmniVChat. They cover omni models, benchmarks, joint audio-video generation, agent systems, and RL. B.1 OMNI MODELS Omni models combine several input and output modalities in one system. GPT-4o (OpenAI, 2024) accepts text, audio, images, and video. Its average audio response latency is 320 milliseconds. The report describes native processing and an earlier cascade for speech transcription, text processing, and audio synthesis. The Gemini Live API (Google, 2026c) processes continuous audio, image, and text streams. It produces spoken responses. Qwen3-Omni (Xu et al., 2025b) uses

sections.content: mixture-of-experts architecture. Its Thinker generates text. Its Talker produces audio tokens. VITA1.5 (Fu et al., 2026) progressively integrates vision and speech. It does not use separate speech recognition or synthesis modules. Baichuan-Omni-1.5 (Li et al., 2025) uses an audio tokenizer. It preserves semantic and acoustic information. Ola (Liu et al., 2025b) uses progressive trainIt aligns language, vision, and audio through video. OmniVinci (Ye et al., 2026) ing strategy. jointly aligns audio-visual embeddings and their temporal structure. Ming-Omni (Inclusion AI et al., 2025) uses modality-speciﬁc routers. The routers send each modalitys tokens to experts in one model. InternLM-XComposer2.5-OmniLive (Zhang et al., 2024) uses separate components for live dialogue. These components handle streaming perception, memory, and reasoning. MiniCPM-o 4.5 (Cui et al., 2026) aligns multimodal inputs and outputs on one timeline. This design supports simultaneous listening and speaking. SeedRealtime (ByteDance Seed, 2026a) uniﬁes audio, video, and text. Its full-duplex model supports real-time multimodal dialogue. D.2 CONSTRUCTION OF OMNIVCHAT-BENCH-HUMAN OmniVChat-Bench-Human tests the transfer claim in 4.3 with 360 human recordings. Each of the twelve single-turn subcategories has 30 instances. The ﬁve multi-turn subcategories are outside its scope. Figure 6 uses the layout of Figure 3 to show this composition. Recordings that fail are corrected or recorded again, then rechecked. Only accepted recordings enter annotation. This process applies the same subcategory deﬁnitions to human speech and real settings. It preserves natural framing and performance. The probe tests whether the same subcategories transfer to recorded dialogues. Annotation starts with three independent captions for each accepted recording. Two captions focus on different evidence, and third includes transcript. The annotation process merges them into one factual record. It retains transcript when any source provides one. sections.content: D.5 DETAILED SUBCATEGORY DEFINITIONS The benchmark contains 17 subcategories: twelve single-turn subcategories and ﬁve multi-turn extensions. The single-turn set has 2,550 instances, each with one clip for one user turn. The multi-turn set has 250 instances and adds memory, retrieval, or updates across turns. The following deﬁnitions cover all 17 subcategories under the ﬁve ability categories in 3. Voice-Connectivity Conﬁrmation (VCC). Initial Connectivity Conﬁrmation (ICC) tests opening connection checks. Mid-Dialogue Connectivity Conﬁrmation (MDCC) extends ICC to later connection checks. Its reply conﬁrms the connection and remains consistent with the earlier dialogue. Fixed clips use direct questions rather than simulate random link loss. Voice Turn-Taking (VTT). User Paused but not Completed (UPC) tests an unﬁnished request amid visual distraction and calls for waiting or brief acknowledgment. User Completed Request (UCR) tests completed request under similar distraction and calls for an answer. Visual Dialogue-Mode Cognition (VDMC). Single-turn Visual Mode Recognition (SVMR) tests user-relative left and right. In these tasks, the users left and right map to the opposite image sides when the camera faces the user. They map to the same image sides when the camera faces outward. Multi-turn Visual Mode Switching (MVMS) extends SVMR by testing the updated left-right mapping after camera change. Reference Comprehension (RC). Anaphoric Reference (AR) resolves pronouns and gestures, while Descriptive Reference (DR) resolves spoken descriptions. Multi-turn Reference Retrieval (MRR) extends both AR and DR by testing recall of information about an object shown earlier. The object leaves the current view, and other topics are discussed before the ﬁnal query. The answer therefore uses earlier visual evidence. Speaker Diarization & Identiﬁcation (SDI). Single-turn Primary Speaker Disambiguation (SPSD) identiﬁes the main user among competing voices. Multi-turn Interactor Shift Tracking (MIST) extends SPSD to changes in the active user. The reply addresses the person who takes over the dialogue. Identity Consistency (IC). Single-turn Identity Consistency (STIC) tests correct model identity in one turn. Multi-turn Identity Consistency (MTIC) extends STIC to identity questions across turns, including misleading user claims. The reply reﬂects the models true identity despite those claims. PLA, AOR, FGC, and ER are themselves subcategories. Their deﬁnitions are in 3. The ﬁve multiturn extensions use the subsystem in 2.2. Figure 3 shows their turn counts and durations.
